chapters.title: Chapter 2: Theories of Exchange Rate Determination

lessons.title: The Balance of Payments Approach: Current Account, Capital Account and the Rupee

children.text: PPP explained why goods prices pull currencies over the long run. Interest rate parity explained how forward rates and carry trades work off interest rate gaps. Neither one tells you where the actual dollars come from, or go, on any given day. That is what the balance of payments approach does: it is India's complete ledger of transactions with the rest of the world, and the gaps in that ledger are what genuinely move the rupee's supply and demand in real time.

body.text: The balance of payments records every transaction between India and the rest of the world. Any shortfall in one part of that ledger must be financed by inflows elsewhere, or by drawing down reserves, and that financing need is what directly drives dollar demand and supply for the rupee.

children.text: What the Balance of Payments Actually Records

markDefs.definition: A systematic record of every economic transaction between residents of a country and the rest of the world over a period, published quarterly by the RBI for India.

children.text: splits into two broad accounts. The current account tracks trade in goods and services, investment income and remittances, essentially, money India earns or spends on an ongoing basis. The capital account tracks investment flows, foreign direct investment, portfolio investment, external borrowings and bank deposits, essentially, money moving in or out to fund assets, not everyday transactions. Because every transaction has to be paid for by something, the two accounts are linked by a simple accounting identity: whatever is not covered by trade and income flows must be financed by capital inflows or by drawing down the RBI's reserves.

body.caption: A simplified balance of payments identity (ignoring the small "errors and omissions" adjustment). A current account deficit must be offset by a capital account surplus, a drawdown of reserves, or both.

children.text: The Current Account: Trade, Services and Remittances

India runs a structural merchandise trade deficit almost every year, it imports far more in goods value than it exports, driven overwhelmingly by crude oil and gold, two commodities India has to buy from abroad in enormous volume regardless of the exchange rate. What partly offsets this is India's other great trade story: a large and consistent services trade surplus, built on IT services, business process outsourcing and software exports, industries where Indian firms earn far more from the world than India spends on services from abroad.

markDefs.definition: Money sent home by people working abroad to family or accounts in their home country. India has been the world's largest recipient of remittances for years, driven heavily by workers in the Gulf and professionals in the US, UK and elsewhere.

children.text: The other major current account cushion is

, money sent home by the enormous Indian diaspora working in the Gulf, North America and elsewhere. These flows are large, steady and, unlike portfolio capital, do not reverse the moment global sentiment turns risk-off, which makes them one of the more stable legs of India's current account.

children.text: The Capital Account: How the Deficit Gets Financed

markDefs.definition: External Commercial Borrowing: funds borrowed by Indian companies from overseas lenders, banks or bond markets, in foreign currency, subject to RBI limits and reporting under FEMA.

children.text: Add up the trade deficit and the services and remittance surplus most years, and India still runs a net current account deficit (CAD), spending more abroad than it earns. That gap has to be financed, and the capital account is where it gets financed: foreign direct investment (FDI) into Indian companies and projects, foreign portfolio investment (FPI) into Indian stocks and bonds,

raised by Indian firms overseas, and deposits from non-resident Indians. When these inflows exceed the current account deficit, India's forex reserves grow. When they fall short, the RBI draws down reserves to bridge the gap, or the rupee weakens to bring supply and demand back into balance on its own.

children.text: Why the Balance of Payments Moves the Rupee

Every dollar an importer needs to pay a foreign supplier, and every dollar an FPI brings in to buy Indian bonds, shows up somewhere in this ledger, and each one is either a source of dollar demand or dollar supply against the rupee. As long as capital account inflows comfortably exceed the current account deficit, the rupee tends to hold steady or even strengthen, there are simply more dollars entering the country than leaving it. The pressure builds when that relationship flips: if the current account deficit widens sharply, say because oil prices spike, and capital inflows dry up at the same time, say because global investors turn risk-averse, the RBI has to either sell dollars from its reserves to plug the gap or allow the rupee to depreciate. Usually it does some of both.

body.text: Economists and the RBI watch the current account deficit as a share of GDP, not just its dollar value. A CAD comfortably under 2 to 2.5% of GDP is usually considered manageable and easily financed by normal capital inflows. Once it climbs meaningfully higher, the rupee becomes far more exposed to any sudden stop in foreign capital.

body.title: Balance the Ledger
body.prompt: India's current account deficit for the year is $30 billion. Capital account inflows (FDI, FPI, ECBs and other flows combined) total $45 billion for the same year. Ignoring errors and omissions, what is the change in the RBI's forex reserves for the year, in billions of dollars? (Enter a negative number if reserves fell.)
body.explanation: Current account (-$30bn) plus capital account (+$45bn) equals +$15bn. Capital inflows more than covered the current account deficit, so the RBI's reserves grew by roughly $15 billion for the year, and the rupee faced no financing-driven pressure to weaken.

body.title: Reading the 2013 Taper Tantrum Through the Balance of Payments
body.scenario: Going into 2013, India's current account deficit had widened to one of its highest levels on record as a share of GDP, driven by elevated gold and oil imports. When the US Federal Reserve signalled it would taper its bond-buying programme in May 2013, FPI money that had been flowing into Indian debt and equity reversed sharply and began leaving. The RBI responded partly by launching a special deposit scheme to attract foreign currency deposits from non-resident Indians at attractive rates, successfully pulling in tens of billions of dollars over a few months.
body.prompt: Using the balance of payments framework, explain why a wide current account deficit made India especially vulnerable to the taper tantrum, and why the NRI deposit scheme was a sensible policy response rather than an unrelated fix.
body.modelAnswer: A wide current account deficit means India needs a correspondingly large and steady capital account inflow just to keep reserves stable, let alone growing. Going into 2013, much of that financing was coming from FPI flows into debt and equity, capital that can leave as fast as it arrives. When the Fed's taper signal triggered a global reversal of FPI flows out of emerging markets, India's financing gap did not just narrow, it flipped into an outright shortfall: a large current account deficit with a capital account that could no longer cover it. That combination forced a sharp rupee depreciation and a scramble to defend it. The special NRI deposit scheme worked precisely because it targeted the accounting identity directly, it created a fresh, large, deliberately incentivised capital account inflow to offset the FPI outflow, buying time for the current account deficit itself to narrow through other measures like gold import curbs. It was not a currency trick, it was balance of payments arithmetic: if the capital account will not fill the gap on its own, policy has to go create the inflow.

points: The balance of payments records every transaction between India and the world, split into the current account (trade, income, remittances) and the capital account (FDI, FPI, borrowings, deposits).
India runs a structural current account deficit most years, driven by oil and gold imports, partly offset by a large services trade surplus and the world's largest remittance inflows.

The capital account exists to finance that deficit. When capital inflows exceed the deficit, reserves grow and the rupee holds steady; when they fall short, the RBI draws down reserves, the rupee weakens, or both.
The current account deficit as a share of GDP, not its raw dollar value, is the number the RBI and economists watch most closely as a gauge of currency vulnerability.

The 2013 taper tantrum showed the framework in action: a wide CAD plus a sudden FPI reversal created a financing gap large enough to force sharp rupee depreciation, until policy deliberately engineered a fresh capital inflow to close it.
